usage: Polite; what you ask the daycare teacher or a helper
반말, to your partner or family at home
Could you change the diaper, please?
More polite/formal with -주시겠어요, to staff you don't know well
Stating it about the baby's routine, not a direct request
examples: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요.
Please change the diaper.
Handing the baby (or a fresh diaper) to the teacher at drop-off
애기 기저귀 찼는데 좀 갈아 주세요.
The baby's diaper is wet — please change it.
찼다 ('it's wet/full') tells them why; 애기 is the cozy spoken form of 아기
등원할 때 기저귀 여유분 가방에 넣어 뒀어요. 필요하면 갈아 주세요.
I put spare diapers in the bag for daycare. Please change him if needed.
Real handoff: 여유분 ('spares') + 갈아 주세요 for the teacher to use as needed
nuance: 기저귀 좀 갈아 주세요 means 'please change the diaper' — 기저귀 ('diaper') + 좀 (politeness softener, NOT 'a little') + 갈아 주세요, from 갈다 ('to replace/swap') + 주다 ('do it for me as a favor'). You say it in 존댓말 to a daycare teacher (선생님), a babysitter (이모님/베이비시터), or a relative who's helping; with your spouse you drop to 기저귀 좀 갈아 줘. The key verb trap for English speakers: the verb is 갈다 ('replace one thing with another'), NOT 바꾸다. 바꾸다 means 'exchange/switch' in the sense of trading or returning a product, so 기저귀 바꿔 주세요 sounds like you want to swap the diaper for a different brand at the store, not change a dirty one — always 기저귀 갈다. A second pitfall is the 직역 trap of building it from English 'change' (변경하다 / 바꾸다); none of those fit. Note the wet/dirty state is described with 차다 (기저귀 찼어요, 'the diaper's full/wet'), and the soiled diaper itself you 갈다. Don't add -을/를 in speech; natives say 기저귀 갈다 with no object particle.

usage: Polite; baby-talk word, what you say to the teacher
반말, to your partner or the baby
Clinical/neutral; what you'd say to a doctor
The pee counterpart; 쉬 = baby-talk for pee
examples: 애기 응가했어요. 기저귀 갈아 주세요.
The baby pooped. Please change the diaper.
응가 + the diaper-change request, the natural pair
오늘 어린이집에서 응가 두 번 했어요? 알림장에 적어 주셔서 봤어요.
Did he poop twice at daycare today? I saw it in the notebook.
응가 ... 했어요 with a count; 알림장 ('daycare notebook')
요즘 변비라서 응가를 며칠째 못 했어요. 이유식 바꿔 볼까 봐요.
He's constipated lately and hasn't pooped for days. I might change his solids.
변비 ('constipation') is the clinical word; 며칠째 ('for several days now')
nuance: 응가했어요 means '(he) pooped' — 응가 (baby-talk/nursery word for poop) + 했어요 (past of 하다 'to do'), so 응가하다 = 'to poop'. This is the word adults actually use WITH or ABOUT babies and toddlers: warm, soft, and non-clinical, said in 존댓말 to a daycare teacher (애기 응가했어요) and 반말 to a spouse (응가했어). Its pee-counterpart is 쉬(하다). The register distinction is the whole point for English speakers: 응가 is nursery language (like 'poo/poo-poo'), 똥 is the plain blunt word ('poop/crap' — fine among adults joking but a bit crude to announce to a teacher about a baby), and 변(便)/대변 is the clinical term ('stool/bowel movement') you'd use at the pediatrician (변 봤어요, 'he had a bowel movement'). Pick by audience: teacher/baby → 응가, doctor → 변/대변. The pitfall is (1) defaulting to 똥 in polite childcare talk (slightly coarse) or (2) over-clinically saying 배변했어요 to a daycare teacher (stiff). Also note the verb is 하다 (응가를 하다), and for 'have a bowel movement' the idiom is 변을 보다 ('to see stool', using 보다, not 하다) — 변 했어요 is wrong; it's 변 봤어요. Constipation is 변비, diarrhea is 설사.

똥 is the blunt word and 싸다 is coarse. For a baby in polite talk use the nursery word: 응가했어요. Save 똥 for casual adult joking.
Saying 변 했어요 for 'had a bowel movement'.

usage: Polite; asking the teacher at pickup how naptime went
Did you nap? / Did he nap?
반말, to the child or your partner
Add 잘 ('well') to ask about quality, not just yes/no
Did you put him down for a nap?
Causative 재우다 — asking if SOMEONE made the baby sleep
examples: 오늘 낮잠 잤어요?
Did he nap today?
A simple pickup question to the daycare teacher
우리 애 낮잠 잘 잤어요? 어제 못 자서요.
Did my child nap well? He couldn't sleep yesterday.
잘 잤어요 asks quality; 어제 못 자서요 gives context
낮잠 안 자고 계속 울었다고요? 아이고, 집에서도 그래요.
He didn't nap and kept crying? Oh dear, he's like that at home too.
Reacting to a teacher's report; 안 자고 ('without sleeping') + 울었다
nuance: 낮잠 잤어요? means 'did (he) take a nap?' — 낮잠 (낮 'daytime' + 잠 'sleep' = 'nap') + 잤어요 (past of 자다 'to sleep'). It's the daily pickup question to a daycare teacher about how naptime went, in 존댓말; to your own child or spouse it drops to 낮잠 잤어?. The crucial distinction English speakers miss is 자다 vs 재우다. 자다 is 'to sleep' (the child does it): 낮잠 잤어요? = 'did he sleep?'. 재우다 is the causative 'to put/make someone sleep' (the adult does it): 낮잠 재웠어요? = 'did you put him down?'. Mixing them flips who's doing the action — asking a teacher 낮잠 재웠어요? specifically asks whether SHE got him down, while 낮잠 잤어요? asks whether the child slept at all. Another note: Korean uses 낮잠을 자다 ('sleep a nap', a cognate-object construction) — you don't say 낮잠을 하다 or 낮잠을 가지다 the way English 'take a nap' might tempt you. Drop the object particle in speech: 낮잠 잤어요. To say 'he fell asleep', it's 잠들었어요, not 잤어요.

Using 자다 for 'fell asleep'.

usage: Polite; telling the teacher or pediatrician about the baby's stage
반말, to a friend or family
Stating the current routine with 먹이다 ('to feed')
The negative, when the baby is still on milk only
examples: 저희 애기 이유식 시작했어요.
Our baby has started solids.
A simple update to the daycare teacher at enrollment
이유식 초기라서 미음이랑 쌀죽 위주로 먹여요.
He's in early weaning, so mostly thin rice porridge.
초기 ('early stage') + 미음/쌀죽 are the first weaning foods
이유식 알레르기 때문에 계란이랑 우유는 아직 안 줬어요. 어린이집에서 주의해 주세요.
Because of allergies we haven't given egg or milk yet. Please be careful at daycare.
Real allergy handoff; 주의해 주세요 ('please be cautious')
nuance: 이유식 시작했어요 means 'we've started baby food / solids' — 이유식 (離乳食, Sino-Korean: 離 'separate' + 乳 'milk' + 食 'food', literally 'weaning food') + 시작했어요 (past of 시작하다 'to begin'). 이유식 is a whole culturally weighty topic in Korea — homemade stage-by-stage purées (초기/중기/후기/완료기, early/mid/late/finishing) are a big deal, and many parents cook fresh batches. You say this in 존댓말 to the daycare teacher or doctor; casually to friends it's 이유식 시작했어. The big distinction: 이유식 is the transitional purée food for babies (~6 months on), NOT 아기 음식 (a vague calque of 'baby food' that Koreans rarely use) and NOT 유아식 — which is the NEXT stage, toddler food (소금/양념 lightly added, ~15 months+). Calling a 2-year-old's meal 이유식 is wrong; that's 유아식. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'baby food' literally as 아기 음식 — natives will understand but it sounds off; the real term is 이유식. To 'feed' the baby it, use 먹이다 (causative of 먹다): 이유식 먹여요, never 이유식 먹어요 (which would mean the baby eats it on his own).

Saying 이유식 먹어요 to mean 'I feed him'.

english: What time should I come pick him up?
usage: What time should I pick him up?
Polite; asking the daycare about pickup time
What time are you picking him up?
By what time do I need to be there?
Asking the deadline with -까지 ('by') + 가야 돼요
Stating you'll do the pickup; -ㄹ게요 announces your intention
examples: 오늘 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요?
What time should I come pick him up today?
Confirming pickup time with the teacher
회사가 늦게 끝나서 6시에 데리러 가도 될까요?
Work ends late — would 6 o'clock be okay to pick him up?
Asking permission for a later pickup with -도 될까요
오늘은 할머니가 데리러 가실 거예요. 다른 사람이 가도 괜찮죠?
Grandma will pick him up today. It's okay if someone else comes, right?
Notifying that a different guardian will collect; 가실 거예요 honorifies grandma
nuance: 몇 시에 데리러 가면 돼요? means 'what time should I come pick (him) up?' — 몇 시 ('what time') + 에 (time particle) + 데리러 (purpose form of 데리다 'to take/bring a person') + 가면 돼요 ('is it okay if I go', from -면 되다 'it suffices to / should'). This is a core daily daycare phrase, in 존댓말 to the teacher. Two big pitfalls. First, 데리러 vs 가지러: 데리러 가다 = 'go to fetch a PERSON' (데리다 is for living people you accompany), while 가지러 가다 = 'go to fetch a THING/object'. English 'pick up' covers both, so learners wrongly say 가지러 가다 for a child — but a child is a person, so it must be 데리러 가다. Saying 애기 가지러 갈게요 treats the baby like a package. Second, the -러 ending attaches to a motion verb (가다/오다) and means 'in order to': 데리러 가다 = 'go in order to fetch'. Don't say 데리고 가다 here — 데리고 가다 means 'take (someone) ALONG with you somewhere' (you + child going together), a different action from going to collect them. To pick up at daycare you 데리러 가다; to bring the child somewhere you 데리고 가다.

usage: Polite; asking the daycare's morning arrival time
By what time do we need to arrive?
Asking the deadline with -까지 + 해야 돼요
We're not sending him in today
examples: 등원 시간이 보통 몇 시예요?
What time is drop-off usually?
Asking the daycare's normal morning schedule
내일은 병원 때문에 좀 늦게 등원할게요.
Tomorrow we'll arrive a bit late because of a doctor's visit.
Notifying a late arrival; 등원하다 = the child arrives at daycare
아침마다 등원 전쟁이에요. 애가 안 가려고 울어서요.
Every morning is a drop-off battle — he cries and won't go.
등원 전쟁 ('drop-off war') is a real parent idiom for the morning struggle
nuance: 등원 시간이 몇 시예요? means 'what time is drop-off (at daycare/kindergarten)?' — 등원 (登園, Sino-Korean: 登 'go up to / attend' + 園 'garden', i.e. 유치원/어린이집) + 시간 ('time'). 등원 is the specialized word for arriving at a 어린이집 (daycare) or 유치원 (kindergarten) — both contain 園 ('garden') — and its opposite is 하원 ('leaving daycare to go home'). The parallel words for regular SCHOOL are 등교/하교 (校 'school'), so a key distinction: use 등원/하원 for little kids in daycare/kindergarten, and 등교/하교 once they're in 초등학교 (elementary) and up. Saying 등교 시간 about a 3-year-old in daycare is a register/word mismatch. The English-speaker pitfall: 'drop-off' has no single verb match, and learners overbuild it (애를 어린이집에 데려다주는 시간) — that's understandable but clunky; the crisp word is 등원. Note 등원하다 = the child arrives (intransitive); to say YOU take/send the child, use the causative 등원시키다 (애 등원시켰어요 = 'I dropped the kid off'). Don't confuse 등원 with 출근 (an adult going to work) — different worlds.

english: He fusses a lot when he's sleepy

I barely got him to sleep

When he fusses, holding and patting him gets him to sleep fast.

usage: Polite; explaining the child's temperament to the teacher

He needs some time to adjust

english: Is there anything I need to pack/bring?

I packed everything in the bag

english: It's the adjustment period, so he leaves daycare early
usage: It's the adjustment period so he leaves early
Polite; explaining the short early days

I'll pick him up early today

Asking the teacher how adjustment is going

This week is the adjustment period, so he leaves at 11.
적응 기간 ('settling-in period') is standard for new daycare kids
적응 기간이라 처음엔 한두 시간만 있다가 하원해요.
During settling-in he stays only an hour or two at first, then goes home.
있다가 ('stay and then') describes the gradual schedule
적응 기간 끝나면 종일반으로 바꿀 거예요. 그때부턴 5시에 데리러 갈게요.

usage: 반말, scolding your own child gently

Oh come on, stop fussing.

Don't throw a fit because I won't buy the toy. Let's talk at home.

english: Did he have a good day at daycare?
usage: Did he have a good day at daycare?
Polite; the standard pickup question to the teacher
Did you have a good day at daycare?
Anything happen today? / Was everything okay?
Shorter open question to the teacher
examples: 오늘 우리 애 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요?
Did our child have a good day at daycare today?
The everyday pickup check-in with the teacher
오늘 잘 지냈어요? 밥은 잘 먹었고요?
Did he do well today? And did he eat okay?
Stacking a second question with -고요 ('and…?')
오늘 친구랑 안 싸우고 잘 지냈어요? 어제 좀 다퉜다고 해서요.

nuance: 오늘 어린이집에서 잘 지냈어요? means 'did (he) spend the day well / have a good day at daycare today?' — 오늘 ('today') + 어린이집 + 에서 (location-of-action particle, 'at') + 잘 ('well') + 지냈어요 (past of 지내다 'to spend time / get along / fare'). This is THE daily pickup question to a daycare teacher in 존댓말 (and to your child in 반말: 잘 지냈어?). The verb 지내다 is the key: it means 'to get on / fare / spend one's time (well or badly)', covering both 'have a good time' and 'get along with people' — 잘 지내다 ('do well, get along'), 어떻게 지냈어요? ('how have you been?'). Mixing 에/에서 is the classic error: use 에 for going-to/existing-at a static point (가다/있다), 에서 for doing something at a place. structuredNuance.t: 'Did (he) spend the day well / have a good day at daycare today?' — 오늘 ('today') + 어린이집 + 에서 (location-of-action particle, 'at') + 잘 ('well') + 지냈어요 (past of 지내다 'to spend time / get along / fare'). This is THE daily pickup question to a daycare teacher in 존댓말 (and to your child in 반말: 잘 지냈어?). The verb 지내다 is the key: it means 'to get on / fare / spend one's time (well or badly)', covering both 'have a good time' and 'get along with people' — 잘 지내다 ('do well, get along'), 어떻게 지냈어요? ('how have you been?'). For 'get along with friends' specifically, 친구랑 잘 지내다.
Don't confuse 지내다 with 지나다 ('to pass by/elapse'). 지내다 asks how he fared; 지나다 is just time elapsing.

Two traps: (1) the particle — actions happening AT a place take 에서, not 에. 어린이집'에서' 지냈어요 (action at daycare); 어린이집'에' would be a destination ('to daycare'), wrong here. The classic error: use 에 for going-to/existing-at a static point (가다/있다), 에서 for doing something at a place. (2) Translating 'have a good day' literally as 좋은 하루 보냈어요? — understandable but 잘 지냈어요? is the idiomatic, warmer phrasing for how a child fared.

Understandable, but the natural pickup phrase is 잘 지냈어요? ('did he fare well / have a good time'). 지내다 is the lived-in verb for how someone got on.

지내다 = 'to fare/spend time/get along'; 지나다 = 'to pass by / elapse'. 잘 지냈어요? asks how he did, not whether time passed. Keep the verbs distinct.
